Danced
dănst
v. (moved in measured steps; in Scripture both the king's worship and the harlot's snare)
Old French dancier. The Hebrew karar at 2 Samuel 6 means to whirl about; the Greek orcheomai is the ordinary word for dancing, used of Herodias' daughter and in the Lord's parable of the children in the marketplace.

Biblical Definition

Two dances stand at the extremes of Scripture. David's: “And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod” (2Sa 6:14). His wife watched and “saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart” (2Sa 6:16), and David's answer was that he would yet be more vile than that. The dance was before the LORD, in a priestly garment, at the return of the ark. The other: “when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod” (Mat 14:6); Mark adds that “the king said unto the damsel, Ask of me whatsoever thou wilt” (Mar 6:22), and a prophet's head was carried in on a charger. Before them, and to please a man — the whole difference is in the two prepositions. Israel had a dance of victory when Miriam took a timbrel and the women followed (Exo 15:20), and the Preacher grants “a time to dance” (Ecc 3:4). Benjamin's wives were seized out of a dance at Shiloh (Jdg 21:23), which the book records without approving. And the Lord's own complaint against His generation was that it would neither dance nor lament (Mat 11:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to dance as to leap or step with measured steps, regulated by music; and notes that the ancient sacred dances were performed in worship, distinct from those of festivity.

expand to see more

DANCE, v.i. To leap or step with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument.

2. To leap and frisk about; to move nimbly or up and down.

DANCE, v.t. To make to dance; to dandle, as an infant.

David danced before the Lord with all his might. 2 Sam. vi.

Key Scripture

2Sa 6:14 — "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod."

2Sa 6:16 — "And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart."

Mat 14:6 — "But when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod."

Ecc 3:4 — "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;"

Modern Corruption

David's dance is used to license whatever a worshipper feels moved to do, and Michal's contempt to silence every objection, though the text specifies both the object and the garment.

expand to see more

Second Samuel 6 is quoted as the charter of unrestrained expression in worship, and the details of the chapter are usually left out. David danced before the LORD — the object is named — and he was girded with a linen ephod, a priestly garment, at the appointed return of the ark to its place. He was not improvising a private ecstasy; he was leading a procession that the earlier part of the same chapter shows him getting badly wrong the first time, when Uzzah died because the ark was carried on a cart instead of on the shoulders of Levites as the law required. The chapter is therefore an unlikely proof text for the view that God accepts any worship offered with sincerity, since it contains one of Scripture's starkest lessons that He does not. Michal's sin was real and is named, but her presence in the chapter does not turn every question about worship into contempt.

The second dance settles the matter from the other side, and it is not settled by squeamishness. Herodias' daughter danced before them, and the text says plainly that she pleased Herod — a girl used by her mother as a lever, a drunken oath sworn before guests, and John the Baptist beheaded in a prison because a king would not lose face. Nothing in Scripture forbids dancing as such; the Preacher grants a time for it, Miriam led one, and the father in the Lord's parable had music and dancing in the house when his son came home. What Scripture does is ask the two questions this word always raises: before whom, and to please whom. Where the answer is God, the ephod is on and the king may be as vile as David was willing to be. Where the answer is a room of men, the end of it is a charger.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew karar (H3769), to whirl, of David; machowl (H4234), a dance, of Miriam and the daughters of Shiloh; Greek orcheomai (G3738), to dance.

expand to see more

Hebrew karar (H3769) — to whirl, to dance; David danced before the LORD with all his might; 2 Samuel 6:14.

Hebrew machowl (H4234) — a round dance; praise him with the timbrel and dance; Psalm 150:4, Exodus 15:20.

Hebrew ephod bad — a linen ephod, the priestly garment David wore in the procession; 2 Samuel 6:14.

Greek orcheomai (G3738) — to dance; the daughter of Herodias, and the children in the marketplace; Matthew 14:6, Matthew 11:17.

Greek choros (G5525) — a band of dancers, dancing; heard by the elder brother from the field; Luke 15:25.

Usage

"“David danced before the LORD with all his might” — the object named, and the ephod on."

"“She despised him in her heart” — and David said he would be yet more vile."

"“Danced before them, and pleased Herod” — the other preposition, and its price."
